questions.text: For a discrete good, what does the reservation price of its first unit represent?

options.a: The price at which market supply becomes zero.
options.b: The highest price at which the consumer is willing to buy one unit rather than none.
options.c: The minimum price the producer must receive to cover fixed costs.
options.d: The lowest price the consumer would ever pay for any unit.

questions.text: For a discrete good, the reservation price of the nth unit represents what?

options.a: The average income of the consumer.
options.b: The additional variable cost of production.
options.c: The incremental willingness to pay for consuming unit n rather than n-1.
options.d: The price of consuming all n units together.

questions.text: Under quasilinear preferences u(x,y) = v(x) + y, with v(0) = 0, what is the reservation price for the first unit?

options.c: v(1) + income.
options.d: v(1) times the quantity of y.

questions.text: Under the same quasilinear preferences, how do we compute the reservation price of the nth unit?

options.a: v(n) - n times income.
options.d: v(n)/n regardless of n.

questions.text: When marginal willingness to pay decreases with each additional unit, how do the reservation prices behave?

options.a: They are weakly decreasing across successive units.
options.b: They increase strictly with every unit.
options.c: They are identical to marginal costs.
options.d: They are all equal to income.

questions.text: If a consumer optimally purchases n units at price p and successive reservation prices are decreasing, what must hold?

options.a: Every reservation price must be below p.
options.b: The (n+1)th reservation price must exceed p.
options.c: The first reservation price must equal p exactly.
options.d: The nth reservation price is at least p and the (n+1)th reservation price is at most p.

questions.text: Why is the demand curve for a discrete good often step-shaped?

options.a: Consumer income changes at every quantity.
options.b: All units are purchased at exactly the same marginal willingness to pay.
options.c: Different additional units become worth purchasing at distinct reservation-price thresholds.
options.d: Market prices are fixed by law.

questions.text: Under quasilinear preferences, how can v(n) be recovered from the demand schedule if v(0)=0?

options.a: Sum the reservation prices for the first n units.
options.b: Multiply the last reservation price by income.
options.c: Sum the market supply prices.
options.d: Integrate the producer's marginal cost curve.

questions.text: What does gross consumer surplus for n discrete units represent?

options.a: Total wealth of all market consumers.
options.b: Total spending on those units.
options.c: The sum of the willingness to pay for those n units before deducting the expenditure on them.
options.d: Profit earned by the seller.

questions.text: What is net consumer surplus when n units are purchased at unit price p?

options.a: The consumer's entire income.
options.b: The sum of the first n reservation prices minus np.
options.c: np minus gross willingness to pay.
options.d: The sum of reservation prices plus np.

questions.text: Why can consumers obtain positive surplus on units they purchase?

options.a: Their monetary income necessarily increases after buying.
options.b: Their willingness to pay for some units exceeds the market price.
options.c: The seller always sells below marginal cost.
options.d: Consumers receive refunds on every purchase.

questions.text: A consumer values three units at €12, €9 and €5 respectively and the market price is €6. What is the consumer's surplus from buying optimally?
Which units will a consumer buy at a uniform price p under quasilinear utility and declining reservation prices?

options.a: Units with marginal willingness to pay at least p.
options.b: Only units with marginal willingness to pay strictly below p.
options.c: Only units whose marginal willingness to pay equals zero.
options.d: Every available unit regardless of willingness to pay.

questions.text: With quasilinear utility and a continuous good x, what interior condition defines inverse demand?

options.a: p(x) = marginal cost of the producer.
options.b: p(x) = v(x)/income.
options.c: p(x) = average willingness to pay regardless of x.

questions.text: For continuous quasilinear demand, gross willingness to pay for x units can be represented by what?

options.a: The derivative of total expenditure.
options.b: The area under inverse demand from zero to x.
options.c: The area under market supply alone.
options.d: The rectangle p times x only.

questions.text: In a price-quantity diagram, consumer surplus at price p and chosen quantity x is what area?

options.a: The entire region to the right of quantity x.
options.b: The rectangle between quantity zero and x below price p.
options.c: The area under inverse demand and above price p up to x.
options.d: The area below the supply curve and above zero.

questions.text: Why does a price increase typically reduce consumer surplus?

options.a: It makes willingness to pay increase mechanically.
options.b: It raises expenditure on remaining purchases and eliminates surplus on some forgone units.
options.c: It always causes total utility to rise.
options.d: It increases consumers' income by the price change.

questions.text: When price increases and quantity demanded falls, which component of lost surplus applies to units still purchased?

options.a: Only the difference in fixed costs.
options.b: The gain from reduced purchases.
options.c: The entire cost of production.
options.d: The extra payment on units that continue to be purchased.

questions.text: Which component of surplus loss after a price increase comes from reduced consumption?

options.a: Surplus previously earned on units no longer purchased.
options.b: Savings on units never previously bought.
options.c: A change in producer's wage bill alone.
options.d: Extra payment on units still purchased.

questions.text: Why is consumer surplus an exact monetary welfare measure under quasilinear preferences with interior numeraire consumption?

options.a: Demand for the non-numeraire good has no income effect.
options.b: Consumer preferences are always homothetic.
options.c: Producers earn zero profit.
options.d: Prices never change.

questions.text: Why may ordinary consumer surplus be an imperfect welfare measure with general preferences?

options.a: Income effects make willingness to pay depend on the consumer's utility or income level.
options.b: Indifference curves cease to exist.
options.c: Demand is always perfectly elastic.
options.d: Producer surplus always equals zero.

questions.text: When is a change in ordinary consumer surplus more likely to approximate a welfare change well?

options.a: When income effects dominate substitution effects.
options.b: When the consumer cannot spend money on other goods.
options.c: When income effects for the good are small.
options.d: When demand is a Giffen curve everywhere.

questions.text: For a quasilinear utility function u(x,y)=v(x)+y, what does the numeraire good y permit?

options.a: Fixing demand for x independently of price.
options.b: Forcing every reservation price to be identical.
options.c: Expressing changes in utility from x in monetary units.
options.d: Eliminating the consumer's budget constraint.

questions.text: If market price falls, what generally happens to ordinary consumer surplus?

options.a: It becomes negative for all buyers.
options.b: It is necessarily unchanged.
options.c: It falls.
options.d: It rises.

questions.text: What is the economic interpretation of consumer surplus under quasilinear preferences?

options.a: The total monetary income received after consumption.
options.b: The producer's avoided fixed costs.
options.c: Net willingness to pay above the amount actually spent.
options.d: The market-clearing value of unsold output.

questions.text: After a price increase, compensating variation (as a positive compensation amount) is what?

options.a: Money removed at old prices to achieve post-change utility.
options.b: The tax revenue from the price increase.
options.c: The firm's additional cost of production.
options.d: Additional money needed at the new prices to restore the initial utility level.

questions.text: After a price increase, equivalent variation (as a positive loss amount) is what?

options.a: The difference between accounting and economic profit.
options.b: The value of the consumer's initial endowment.
options.c: Additional money needed at new prices to regain old utility.
options.d: Money that could be taken away at the old prices to reduce welfare to its post-increase level.

questions.text: Which price vector is used in the compensating variation calculation after a price increase?

options.a: The old prices only.
options.b: The average of the old and new prices necessarily.
options.c: A price vector with both goods' prices set to zero.
options.d: The new prices.

questions.text: Which price vector is used in the equivalent variation calculation after a price increase?

options.a: The old prices.
options.b: A price vector equal to marginal costs.
options.c: The new prices only.
options.d: A vector with every price doubled.

questions.text: Why can compensating and equivalent variation differ under general preferences?

options.a: They differ only when preferences are irrational.
options.b: Income effects make the money metric depend on the reference utility level and prices.
options.c: Compensating variation measures producers and equivalent variation measures consumers.
options.d: The two definitions always use the same utility and price vectors.

questions.text: When are compensating and equivalent variation equal in the slide's standard case?

options.a: Under quasilinear preferences with no income effect for the affected good.
options.b: Whenever a price rises, regardless of preferences.
options.c: Only when expenditure is zero.
options.d: Only when the good is Giffen.

questions.text: How are compensating and equivalent variation related to the expenditure function e(p,u)?

options.a: They are both derivatives of profit with respect to input prices.
options.b: They can only be computed from market supply.
options.c: They are differences in minimum expenditures evaluated at appropriate prices and utility levels.
options.d: They are the same as firm revenue and profit.

questions.text: Suppose p0 and p1 are initial and new prices, with utility u0 before and u1 after a price increase. What is positive compensating variation?
Under the same notation, what is positive equivalent variation?
Why is it useful to distinguish ordinary surplus from CV and EV?

options.a: CV and EV ignore consumer preferences.
options.b: CV and EV are exact money-metric welfare changes using the expenditure function, whereas ordinary surplus may be approximate.
options.c: Ordinary surplus always gives more accurate welfare measurement.
options.d: CV and EV measure only producer welfare.

questions.text: If reservation prices are €14, €10 and €7, and the uniform price is €8, how many units maximize net surplus?

options.a: Two.
options.b: One.
options.c: Three.
options.d: Zero.

questions.text: If demand shifts outward because of higher income, why is the original area under demand not automatically an exact welfare index?

options.a: The demand curve becomes identical to marginal cost.
options.b: Willingness to pay can vary with income, violating the quasilinear simplification.
options.c: Consumer surplus becomes independent of quantity.
options.d: The price must be zero.

questions.text: Which statement is correct about willingness to pay for a discrete additional unit?

options.a: It is always larger than the consumer's total income.
options.b: It equals the seller's average fixed cost.
options.c: It equals the market equilibrium price for all consumers.
options.d: It is determined by indifference between buying that unit and not buying it, given the remaining spending possibilities.

questions.text: If a price decline induces additional purchases, where do the gains on the newly bought units appear in the surplus diagram?

options.a: Only above the original price line.
options.b: In the area between demand and the new price over the additional quantity range.
options.c: Entirely below the supply curve.
options.d: Only on the units purchased before the price decline.

questions.text: Under quasilinear utility, why can market demand reveal marginal willingness to pay?

options.a: Marginal willingness to pay equals average cost.
options.b: All consumers have identical marginal utility of income by definition regardless of numeraire.
options.c: The income effect is always large and positive.
options.d: The marginal utility of x expressed in numeraire units equals its inverse demand price.

questions.text: If a consumer values two units at €10 and €6 and market price is €5, what is total consumer surplus from buying both?
For the displayed price increase, what do the shaded areas R and T represent together?

options.a: The total gain in producer surplus.
options.b: The seller's total fixed costs.
options.c: The total loss in consumer surplus.
options.d: The entire new consumer expenditure.
